title: So, let’s make our own dataset
gist: A community Hugging Face Blog tutorial walks through a self-contained Python script that collects metadata (not content) for the top 1,000 most-downloaded Hugging Face dataset repositories via the Hub API, and uses the resulting Sept 9, 2026 snapshot to teach methodological discipline around missing data, snapshot bias, and the limits of the Hub's rolling 30-day download metric.

insights.claim: The tutorial's core engineering principle is to always keep the raw collected API response (saved untouched to a RAWDATA folder) physically separate from any derived/processed dataset, so any downstream anomaly can be traced back to what the source actually returned versus what was added during processing.
insights.speaker: Hugging Face
insights.so_what: A reusable due-diligence checklist item when evaluating any dataset/analytics vendor: ask whether they retain and can show the original unprocessed source snapshot.
insights.quote: This is a habit worth getting into early: keep what you collected separate from what you changed.

insights.claim: The collection script requests only one page of up to 1,000 dataset repositories sorted by trailing 30-day downloads and does not implement pagination, so it captures only the most-downloaded slice of Hugging Face's dataset catalog, not a census of the whole Hub; a full-Hub crawl would require the official huggingface_hub SDK, which handles pagination and rate limiting.
insights.speaker: Hugging Face
insights.so_what: Anyone building analytics or a competitive index off Hugging Face's public dataset metadata needs to know a naive single-page pull only covers top-1,000-by-downloads, understating the long tail.
insights.locator: First, ask Hugging Face for the information

insights.claim: After writing the processed dataset to disk, the script reloads the file and compares it record-for-record against the in-memory data, raising an error if they don't match exactly, to guarantee the delivered file is actually intact rather than silently truncated or corrupted.
insights.speaker: Hugging Face
insights.so_what: A concrete, low-cost data-integrity pattern (write-then-reload-and-diff) worth expecting from any serious data pipeline before trusting its output.
insights.quote: That's a simple check, but it means we're actually testing the file someone will use.
insights.locator: Check it before calling it finished

insights.claim: The script deliberately preserves missing values (e.g. absent download counts or citation text) as null rather than coercing them to zero, because a missing count and a reported count of zero carry different meanings and silently zero-filling would corrupt any resulting statistics.
insights.speaker: Hugging Face
insights.so_what: A general data-quality red flag to check for in any vendor dataset: does it distinguish 'unknown/not reported' from 'zero', or does it silently blend the two and understate true incidence rates?
insights.quote: So the script keeps missing counts as missing. It doesn't quietly turn them into zero just to make the column look tidy.

insights.claim: Requesting the 'citation' field from the Hugging Face API does not guarantee every repository has a value for it; it is a documented but frequently absent field, and an empty or absent tag list means the API response lacked that information, not that the underlying repository necessarily lacks it (the article notes the API's returned tags haven't been independently verified against actual repository files).
insights.speaker: Hugging Face
insights.so_what: Caution against treating Hugging Face Hub API metadata completeness as ground truth about what's actually inside a dataset repository.
insights.locator: So what does processing actually mean?

insights.claim: The article distinguishes task categories (what a dataset can be used for, e.g. text classification) from topics/subjects (what a dataset covers, e.g. cybersecurity), arguing these are conceptually different taxonomies that should be tracked in separate fields rather than conflated.
insights.speaker: Hugging Face
insights.so_what: A modeling distinction relevant to anyone building a dataset/content taxonomy or search index on top of Hub metadata.
insights.quote: Also, task categories and topics aren't quite the same thing. “Text classification” describes something you can do with a dataset. “Cybersecurity” describes a subject it might cover.
insights.locator: So what does processing actually mean?

insights.claim: In the article's own 1,000-record Hugging Face dataset snapshot collected September 9, 2026 (top repositories by trailing-30-day downloads), 369 of 1,000 records returned no format tags at all, and 987 of 1,000 returned no citation text through the API request.
insights.speaker: Hugging Face
insights.so_what: Quantifies how sparse structured metadata (format, citation) still is across even the most-downloaded datasets on the leading open dataset hub, a gap for anyone trying to build automated dataset-quality or provenance scoring on top of Hub metadata alone.

insights.claim: In the same 1,000-record snapshot, format:parquet was the second most common declared format tag at 215 repositories (21.5% of the sample) while format:imagefolder was the most common at 328 repositories, based on formats_counts.csv output from the run.
insights.speaker: Hugging Face
insights.so_what: A concrete, dated data point on file-format adoption among the most-downloaded Hugging Face datasets, useful as a baseline to compare against later snapshots for format-adoption trend tracking.
insights.quote: We can say that 215 of the 1,000 repositories had a format:parquet tag in that response. That is 21.5% of our selected sample. The most common returned format tag was imagefolder, appearing in 328 repositories.

insights.claim: One example record from the September 9, 2026 snapshot, the dataset repository KakologArchives/KakologArchives, reported 2,509,960 downloads over the trailing 30 days and 82 likes, yet returned a null citation field and only Japanese-language and text-classification tags — illustrating that even very high-traffic Hugging Face datasets commonly lack citation metadata via the public API.
insights.speaker: Hugging Face
insights.so_what: A concrete illustration that download popularity on Hugging Face does not correlate with metadata completeness (citation, provenance), a due-diligence gap for downstream dataset consumers.
insights.locator: JSONL for the dataset, CSV for the reports

themes.theme: Limits of the Hugging Face download metric

insights.claim: Hugging Face's Hub API 'downloads' field measures downloads over a rolling trailing 30-day window rather than a lifetime total, so it is not a cumulative popularity measure and resets/shifts continuously as the window rolls forward.
insights.speaker: Hugging Face
insights.so_what: Analysts building download-based popularity or momentum signals for Hugging Face models/datasets must treat the metric as a trailing-30-day rate, not a stock of total historical downloads.
insights.quote: The API's downloads field covers the last 30 days; it is not a lifetime total.

insights.claim: Because the Hugging Face downloads figure is a rolling 30-day window, simply subtracting the download counts from two snapshots taken weeks apart does not correctly measure new downloads that occurred between the two collection dates, and a repository dropping out of a top-1,000-by-downloads ranking does not imply it was deleted — only that its trailing-30-day downloads fell relative to others.
insights.speaker: Hugging Face
insights.so_what: A specific methodological trap to avoid when building any time-series or momentum comparison off repeated Hugging Face Hub snapshots — naive snapshot-diffing will produce misleading 'new download' or 'delisting' signals.
insights.quote: A repository dropping out of the top 1,000 doesn't mean it was deleted. Each download count covers a rolling 30 day window, so subtracting two snapshots won't tell you how many new downloads happened between runs.
insights.locator: Where do we go from here?

insights.claim: Hugging Face downloads are not unique-user counts, and the article's own owner-level download totals are sums of repository-level download counts, not a measure of distinct downloaders — so aggregated owner/organization download totals overstate the number of unique users reached.
insights.speaker: Hugging Face
insights.so_what: Reinforces that any 'reach' narrative built from Hugging Face download totals (e.g. for an organization's dataset portfolio) should be read as request volume, not audience size.
insights.quote: Download totals are sums of repository counts, not unique downloaders.
